title: Reason Through SAT Survey Questions
description: Evaluate survey samples, limit conclusions to the correct population, and interpret margin of error as a plausible range.

questions.stem_html: A survey in Millbrook aims to estimate the views of all library card holders. Which sampling method best supports that goal?
questions.explanation_html: The complete list covers the population, and random selection gives population members an opportunity to be included.
questions.variation: Choose a random sample from the intended population
choices: Randomly select 80 people from the complete list of library card holders.
Survey the first 80 after-school club members to volunteer.
Survey only after-school club members.
Survey every after-school club members met at one location.

distractor_notes.B: Volunteer responses may differ from the population.
distractor_notes.C: This leaves out other members of the population.
distractor_notes.D: The location and group restrict who can be included.

questions.stem_html: A researcher in Brighton randomly selects 50 students enrolled in band from a complete list of that group. All selected people answer. To which population can the results most reasonably be generalized?
questions.explanation_html: The randomly sampled population consists of students enrolled in band in Brighton. The results support generalization to that population.
questions.variation: Keep every restriction of the sampled group
choices: All students in Brighton
All students enrolled in band nationwide
Only the individuals who answered
All students enrolled in band in Brighton

distractor_notes.B: Extends the geography beyond the sampling frame.
distractor_notes.C: A representative random sample can estimate its source population.

questions.stem_html: A study in Oak Crossing needs the views of all town employees. It randomly selects 60 from a complete list, but most selected people who cannot attend daytime meetings never respond. What concern matters most?
questions.explanation_html: Random selection helps at the invitation stage. When response depends on availability, the group that answered can underrepresent people with different schedules.
questions.variation: Recognize systematic nonresponse after random selection
choices: Random selection guarantees an unbiased response group.
Selecting more people guarantees the same view from everyone.
The people who answered may differ systematically from the people who did not answer.
Only opinions from outside the population are affected.

distractor_notes.A: Initial selection does not fix systematic nonresponse.
distractor_notes.B: Sample size does not fix systematic missing responses.
distractor_notes.D: The missing voices belong to the population of interest.

questions.stem_html: A town wants to estimate resident support for adding a weekend bus route. Which survey question would best serve that purpose?
questions.explanation_html: The neutral question asks about support without suggesting an answer or combining it with another topic.
questions.variation: Choose neutral wording to estimate opinion
choices: Wouldn’t a weekend route make our town more welcoming?
Should we avoid wasting money on weekend buses?
Do you support or oppose adding a weekend bus route?
Do you ride a bus now, and should the town add a weekend route?

distractor_notes.A: Suggests that respondents ought to support the route.
distractor_notes.B: Frames opposition as the responsible choice.
distractor_notes.D: Asks about current use and opinion in a single answer.

questions.stem_html: A random sample of eighth graders found 62% support for a longer lunch break, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. What is the lower endpoint of the estimated percentage range? Enter the number without the percent sign.
questions.explanation_html: Subtract the margin of error in percentage points: 62 − 4 = 58. The estimated interval is 58% to 66%.
questions.variation: Apply the margin and preserve the population scope

questions.stem_html: Two surveys use equally representative random samples of 60 and 240 students from the same school, with similar response rates and the same neutral question. Which conclusion about precision is best supported?
questions.explanation_html: With the sampling method and response rates comparable, the larger random sample generally reduces sampling variability.
questions.variation: Distinguish precision from selection and certainty
choices: The 240-student sample should generally give a smaller margin of error.
The smaller sample should have a smaller margin of error.
The larger sample guarantees that the estimate equals the population result.
Both margins of error must be identical.

distractor_notes.B: Reverses the effect of sample size on precision.
distractor_notes.D: Ignores the difference in number of observations.

questions.stem_html: A random sample of regular bus riders found 47% support for a weekend bus route, with a margin of error of 5 percentage points. Which interpretation is best supported?
questions.explanation_html: Add and subtract 5 points from 47%. The resulting 42% to 52% is an estimate for the sampled population.
questions.variation: Apply the margin and preserve the population scope
choices: Exactly 47% of all regular bus riders support it.
The estimated share of all regular bus riders who support it is between 42% and 52%.
The estimated share is between 47% and 52%.
The estimated share of everyone in the country is between 42% and 52%.

distractor_notes.A: Treats a sample estimate as exact.
distractor_notes.C: Applies the margin only above the estimate.
distractor_notes.D: Extends the estimate beyond the sampled population.
